findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label rather than a hook, burying the actual hook in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of GRAPHQL SCHEMA DESIGN. Most GraphQL outages are not resolver bugs — they are schema decisions made in a hurry."
findings.fix: Lead with the hook and demote the label: "Most GraphQL outages are not resolver bugs — they are schema decisions made in a hurry. (Part 2 of GRAPHQL SCHEMA DESIGN.)"

findings.summary: The safe/breaking table says changing a field's type is breaking, and a callout three blocks later says a field type change is safe, with nothing distinguishing wrapper changes from named-type changes.
findings.evidence: Table row: ["Change a field's type","breaking"]. Callout "Tighten, Never Loosen": "`[Post]` to `[Post!]!` is safe for clients — a stronger guarantee".
findings.fix: Change the table row to "Change a field's named type" and add a bullet under it: "Wrapper changes are a separate axis — tightening nullability is safe, loosening is breaking", so the callout reads as the stated exception rather than a contradiction.

findings.summary: The cheat-sheet and trade-off sections are split across two pages in the wrong order, so the page titled "Trade-offs and the Cheat Sheet" arrives after its own content has already been delivered and then repeats the wrapper material.
findings.evidence: Page 4 is titled "Nullability Lines, Schema Smells, and Errors as Data (cont.)" yet contains "Trade-offs Worth Naming" and "Abstract & Wrapper Cards" with the array `T` / `T!` / `[T]` / `[T!]` / `[T]!` / `[T!]!` plus "`[T]` nullable list of nullable items"; page 5, titled "Trade-offs and the Cheat Sheet", then opens with "List Shapes At A Glance" covering `[String]`, `[String!]`, `[String]!`, `[String!]!` again and contains no trade-off section at all.
findings.fix: Move the "Trade-offs Worth Naming" table and the "Abstract & Wrapper Cards" section (table + array diagram + bullets) from page 4 onto page 5 ahead of "Bubbling In One Breath", and delete the duplicate "List Shapes At A Glance" table, keeping only the `[T]`/`[T!]!` wrapper card; leave page 4 ending at "Union Growth Defence".

findings.summary: The `[Post!]!` list-resilience claim describes an impossible outcome, since a non-null list cannot itself be nullified — the error bubbles past the list to the nearest nullable ancestor.
findings.evidence: "`[Post!]!`: one bad item nullifies the whole list" (contrast with page 3: "Null bubbling reaches the root")
findings.fix: Reword to: "`[Post!]!`: one bad item nullifies the list, and because the list is non-null the null keeps climbing to the nearest nullable ancestor (the root if there is none)". Reserve "nullifies the whole list" for `[Post!]`.

findings.summary: The variable-position rule is stated as absolute, but the spec's IsVariableUsageAllowed permits a nullable variable in a non-null position when the variable or the location has a default value.
findings.evidence: "A declaration must be at least as strict as the argument" / "`$x: String` cannot feed `arg: String!`"
findings.fix: Add the exception: `$x: String = "a"` (or a location with a default) is accepted at `String!` today; a strict-mode RFC would remove that allowance. Keep the no-default example as the illustration.

findings.summary: "Persisted queries" is presented twice as a production control without ever being defined anywhere in the handbook.
findings.evidence: "Commonly disabled in production with persisted queries" and "Depth limits and cost analysis are not in the spec" under "Guarding The Endpoint"; the term appears nowhere else in the part and in no earlier chapter.
findings.fix: Add a bullet defining it before first use: "Persisted queries: the client sends a hash of a pre-registered query, so only known operations execute."

findings.summary: `@deprecated` is stated to work only on fields and enum values, but the spec has allowed it on arguments and input object fields since the October 2021 release.
findings.evidence: "Works on fields and on enum values alike"; spec: `directive @deprecated(reason: String = "No longer supported") on FIELD_DEFINITION | ARGUMENT_DEFINITION | INPUT_FIELD_DEFINITION | ENUM_VALUE`
findings.fix: Change to "Works on fields, enum values, arguments, and input fields (arguments/input fields only if nullable or defaulted)" — relevant because the same page's argument-migration advice depends on it.

findings.summary: The page tells the reader to tighten an argument to non-null after adding it, while asserting two bullets earlier that making an argument non-null is breaking, with no resolution of the conflict.
findings.evidence: "Making an argument non-null is breaking" vs. "Add it nullable with a default, then tighten" (page 5 table repeats "Input / argument … Breaking: nullable to non-null")
findings.fix: Qualify the tightening step: making a defaulted argument non-null keeps working for queries that omit it and only breaks callers that pass an explicit `null`; without a default it is unconditionally breaking.

findings.summary: "An output type can never be an argument" is false as stated: scalars and enums are both input and output types and are legal argument types.
findings.evidence: "An output type can never be an argument" / "Define a parallel `input` type instead"
findings.fix: Restate as "Object, interface, and union types can never be arguments" (only scalars, enums, and input objects are input types).

findings.summary: A catch-all `scalar JSON` is said to kill introspection, but introspection still reports it normally — what is lost is structure for codegen and tooling.
findings.evidence: "`scalar JSON` catch-all kills introspection and codegen"
findings.fix: Reword to "`scalar JSON` catch-all makes the payload opaque to introspection-driven tooling and degrades codegen to `any`".

findings.summary: The page opens with a naming/versioning callout that belongs to the previous page's change-safety topic, before any of the page's own subject matter is introduced.
findings.evidence: Page 3's first block is the cloud callout "Names Are Forever": "A bad type name outlives a bad field implementation, because renaming anything is always a break" — placed above the "Nullability Extremes" heading.
findings.fix: Move the "Names Are Forever" callout to page 2, next to the safe/breaking table where renaming is listed as breaking, and start page 3 with the "Nullability Extremes" heading.

findings.summary: The "Cap Every List" callout restates the unbounded-list smell already made on the previous page, presenting it as new material.
findings.evidence: Page 3 bullet: "Unbounded `[Post!]!` with no `first` is a DoS surface". Page 4 callout: "A bare `[Post!]!` with no `first` argument is a denial-of-service surface."
findings.fix: Drop the page-3 bullet and keep only the page-4 callout (which adds the Connection remedy), or cut the callout and append "bound it and wrap it in a Connection" to the page-3 bullet.
